topics.title: Rendering and re-renders
topics.notes: Crazy how 'prop chnages' are not why React components re-render and it's actually due to state changes. Apparently prop chnages is a common misconception. Most times when a component's prop changes, it's because the parent's state changed and that's what's actually causing the re-render

topics.title: Effects, and when not to use them
topics.notes: Only watched the video and not the reading. Still learned that useEffects should not be a go to for everything. They should be used when you need to do something after a render, like fetching data or updating the DOM. If you can do it during render, then do it during render like event-specific logic.

topics.title: Refs, reducers, and custom hooks
topics.notes: useReducer can be used to manage state and state actions in a modular way. (Refer to screenshot "useReducerExample.png") useRef can be used to store mutable values that do not cause re-renders when updated. Custom hooks can be used to extract and reuse logic across components.

topics.title: Context
topics.notes: Can be used to pass data down the component tree without having to pass props down manually at every level. It can be used for global state management, theming, and more. You can use useReducer with useContext (create a context that holds state and one that holds dispatch).

topics.title: Memoization and the React Compiler
topics.notes: There was an update in Dec 2024 to the React compiler so that your code iss automatically memoized upon build. This means that you no longer have to use React.memo or useMemo in most cases. The compiler will automatically memoize your components and hooks for you. This is a huge performance improvement and will make your code faster and more efficient.

topics.title: What's new in React 19
topics.notes: React 19 includes a lot of support for async rendering, including Suspense and use() for data fetching, useAction() for handling data fetching actions, and a new concurrent mode that allows React to interrupt rendering to work on other tasks. This will make your app more responsive and improve the user experience. Could go back and look into this more.

questions.question: What's the difference between data from a server and state that only lives in the app?
questions.answer: Server data lives in the database, and the app only holds a cached copy that can go stale, so it has to be fetched, cached, refetched and kept in sync. In this app that's the topics and the current week, handled by TanStack Query. App-only state, like the search text, the active tab or which page is open, exists only in the browser and is owned by React (useState or context). Nothing outside the app can change it.

questions.question: What's an optimistic update, and what happens when it fails?
questions.answer: You update the screen right away as if the save already worked, instead of waiting for the server. Here, clicking a status icon saves a snapshot of the topics, then writes the new status into the cache in onMutate. If the PUT fails, onError puts the snapshot back, so the task jumps back to its old tab. Either way, onSettled refetches to match the server.

questions.question: What does an error boundary catch, and what doesn't it catch?
questions.answer: It catches errors thrown while rendering the components below it, including in lifecycle methods and constructors, and a useSuspenseQuery whose fetch fails. It doesn't catch errors in event handlers, in async code like setTimeout or a fetch in useEffect, in server-side rendering, or in the boundary itself. Mutation errors don't reach it unless you rethrow them during render.

questions.question: Why would you load part of an app only when it's needed?
questions.answer: So the first load is smaller and faster. Code for a page the user might never open, like Stats or this Flashcards page, goes into its own chunk with lazy() and is only downloaded when it first renders. Suspense shows a fallback while that chunk loads.

questions.question: What's a compound component? Show me yours.
questions.answer: A parent component plus child parts that share state through context, so you arrange the pieces however you like instead of passing lots of props. Mine is TopicCard: <TopicCard topic={task}> puts the topic and setStatus into context, and TopicCard.Header, TopicCard.Status and TopicCard.Notes read from it. TaskList puts Header and Status in one row and Notes underneath.
